children.text: The capital of Aurora province, facing the Pacific on Luzon's east coast, is regarded as the birthplace of Philippine surfing. The waves of Sabang Beach, the cliff scenery of Dicasalarin Cove, and the history of the
Siege of Baler combine to make it a popular weekend getaway.
Baler is a small Pacific coast town about
230km

northeast of Manila, reachable only by crossing the Sierra Madre mountains. It is the capital of Aurora province and is known as the hometown of Philippine Commonwealth President Manuel L. Quezon and his wife, Aurora Quezon. With rugged mountains to the west and the open Pacific to the east, the area was isolated for a long time, and it still retains an atmosphere suited to simple surf camps and homestays rather than large resorts.
Baler is considered the birthplace of Philippine surfing because in the

, the crew filming the movie Apocalypse Now shot surfing scenes here and left their surfboards behind. The river-mouth break where they filmed came to be called "Charlie's Point" after a line from the film, and local children who later rode the leftover boards started the surfing village that exists today. The waves of Sabang Beach, breaking over a sandy bottom in front of the shore, are well suited for beginners taking lessons.
Baler also carries real historical weight. During the Philippine Revolution in
, around 50 Spanish soldiers were besieged inside Baler Church and held out for about 337 days until
June 1899
, refusing to believe that Spain had already ceded the Philippines to the United States. The church and museum that were the stage for this "Siege of Baler" still stand in the town center.

Baler suits beginners who want to learn to surf, weekend travelers looking for uncrowded beaches and waterfalls, and anyone who enjoys history. Keep in mind that because the coast faces the open Pacific directly, the water is a deep blue rather than the transparent turquoise of Boracay, and rough surf days are common.
Baler is a small town covering about 92.55 km² with a population of about 44,700 (
census), yet on
August 6, 2023
, Republic Act No. 11957 officially recognized it as the "Birthplace of Philippine Surfing," and on

, a Baler branch of the National Museum of the Philippines opened. The church, Quezon Park, and museum in the town center can be explored on foot, and Sabang Beach is reached by tricycle; for the waterfall and giant tree in San Luis and Maria Aurora to the west and Diguisit and Dicasalarin on the east coast, the most efficient approach is to rent a vehicle and cover each area in a half-day trip.
Sabang Beach,
5–10 minutes
from town by tricycle, is lined with surf instructors and board rental shops. A
1-hour
lesson (board included) costs about

, and the mornings, when the waves are gentler, are best for beginners. As your skills improve, you can move on to the reef off Cemento Beach near the fishing port or to Charlie's Point at the river mouth, but both have coral and rock bottoms and suit only intermediate surfers and above.

Hidden beyond a coastal mountain road southeast of town, this crescent-shaped beach with its green cliffs and white lighthouse is Baler's signature view. Because the way in passes through a private road, there is an entrance fee (about

), and climbing the viewpoint stairs behind the beach gives you a view over the whole cove. Tricycles can't manage the final climb, so you go in by habal-habal (motorcycle taxi) or van, and since the road has no lighting, head out before
. Guests of Costa Pacifica resort pay a reduced entrance fee of about
This waterfall in neighboring San Luis is about
high, and you reach it by walking
30–45 minutes
from the parking area, crossing the river several times. The water is cold and the current strong, so it's better to enjoy the spray than to swim. It lies about
15km
southwest of Baler town (
30–40 minutes
by car); you must pay an environmental fee of about
at the registration area and then go in with a guide (about
per group).

blocks.title: Baler Church and the Siege Museum

children.text: San Luis Obispo de Tolosa Church (Baler Church), where Spanish troops held out for 337 days in
, is free to enter. Right next door in Quezon Park, the Museo de Baler opened in
and features exhibits on the siege, President Quezon's belongings and official car, and a
marker identifying the site of his birthplace. It is open
, and admission is with the Baler environmental tourism fee ticket (
per person).
This giant balete tree (a type of banyan) stands in Balete Park in Barangay Quirino, in neighboring Maria Aurora, and is said to be over 600 years old and about
tall. It is about
20–30 minutes
by car from Baler town, and the entrance fee is about

. Its famous feature is the hollow between its roots, big enough for around 10 people, but recent typhoons have broken off large branches and some visitors report that going inside isn't what it used to be, so follow the on-site guidance.
From this hill beside Cemento fishing port, east of town, you can take in Baler Bay and Sabang Beach at a glance. Local lore says residents fled to this hill during the tidal wave of
. At the foot of the hill stand a monument and marker commemorating that tidal wave, the "Tromba Marina," and the entrance fee is about

blocks.title: Diguisit Beach and the coastal drive

children.text: About
10km

east of town on the way to Dicasalarin, this rocky beach is striking for the waves crashing against its rocks. The sun rises behind rock islets offshore, making it a popular sunrise photo spot, and the small Diguisit (Natulo) Falls is right by the roadside. A little farther on, Dinadiawan Beach in Dipaculao has clear water that's good for swimming.

blocks.title: National Museum of the Philippines, Baler branch

children.text: Opened in Barangay Reserva on

, to coincide with Philippine–Spanish Friendship Day, this is the National Museum's 22nd branch and its first in Central Luzon. It has three permanent galleries: one on Aurora's nature, biodiversity, and indigenous knowledge; the "Cruce de Caminos" gallery on the history of Philippine–Spanish exchange; and an art gallery hung with works by Filipino masters. Admission is free, and it is open daily
(closed on government-declared holidays); it is run by the same institution as the
National Museum of the Philippines
in Manila.

Several direct buses to Baler run daily from the Genesis and JoyBus terminal in Cubao, Manila. The trip takes about
5–7 hours
, and fares are about
on a regular air-conditioned bus and about
on the roomier JoyBus.
Departures from Cubao are concentrated in the
window, with additional trips at
and

, and
. Buses from Baler Central Terminal to Manila depart in the
window (as of

Genesis official website
or ask at the terminal.
Tickets sell out quickly on weekends and holidays, so booking online or buying in advance at the terminal is recommended.
You can also travel to Cabanatuan (Nueva Ecija) and transfer to a van bound for Baler, which takes about
3–4 hours
from Cabanatuan.
From Cabanatuan Central Terminal (D.S. Garcia Street), Genesis buses and vans to Baler run from early morning until the afternoon, with fares of about
. If you're coming from Clark or northern Luzon, transferring here is convenient.
Take the NLEX and SCTEX toward Nueva Ecija, then cross the Sierra Madre mountain road (the Baler–Bongabon road). It takes about
5–6 hours
; the mountain section has many sharp curves and can have rockfalls on rainy days, so daytime driving is recommended.
On
March 31, 2026
, the Cabanatuan section of the CLLEX (Central Luzon Link Expressway) opened, so Tarlac to Cabanatuan now takes only about
20 minutes
, and the road is toll-free until
December 2026
. From Cabanatuan there are two routes, one through Rizal and Pantabangan over to Maria Aurora and the other along the Bongabon–Baler road, and the distance from Manila is about
There are no scheduled flights to Baler. If you are coming from overseas, Clark International Airport (CRK) is the closest, and it is about
4–5 hours
by vehicle from the airport.
Neighboring San Luis has a small airport with a
runway (Dr. Juan C. Angara Airport, BQA), but with no scheduled flights it can only be used by charter planes. If you land at Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) in Manila, allow about
1–2 hours
to reach the Cubao terminal by Grab or taxi.
From Baguio, Genesis and JoyBus run 1–3 direct trips to Baler a day, taking about
6–9 hours
. With so few trips, it's best to book ahead on weekends.

From Clark International Airport (CRK) or Angeles, take a bus bound for Cabanatuan from Dau Terminal, then transfer to a van to Baler. Genesis also runs an SM Pampanga (San Fernando)–Baler route, so check the schedule. By car, it's about
4–5 hours
via SCTEX and CLLEX.
A tricycle between town and Sabang Beach costs about
per ride (shared). To visit the waterfall, the Millennium Tree, and Dicasalarin in one day, it's convenient to charter a tricycle (about
) or a van.
For a group of around 10, chartering a van for the day (about
) is economical.
Baler's seasonal pattern differs from that of western Luzon. Because it faces the Pacific, the waves are best during the northeast monsoon (Amihan) season of
October–February
, making this the surfing season, though it also rains often at this time.
March–May
, when the sea calms down, is the best time to relax and swim at the beach, and accommodation fills up early during the Holy Week holidays.
June–October

falls within typhoon season, and Luzon's east coast is often where typhoons make landfall. During this time, mountain roads can be blocked or waves can grow dangerously large, so be sure to check PAGASA forecasts before setting out. Surfing competitions are usually held around
February
, coinciding with Aurora Day (the birthday of Aurora Quezon,
February 19
), when the town has an especially festive atmosphere.
Rain is frequent year-round, with annual rainfall reaching about 3,360mm, and
October–December
is the wettest period. Temperatures are coolest in
January
, at around
by day and
at night, and climb to
by day in
May–August
. On
November 9, 2025

, Super Typhoon Uwan (international name Fung-wong) made landfall in Dinalungan to the north, collapsing part of Baler's seawall and cutting the coastal road in the Dipaculao section, and a state of calamity was declared for the entire province. The main festivals are the Suman Festival and surfing competition during Aurora Day week in
mid-February
(the 18th edition in
opened on
February 13
) and the Philippine–Spanish Friendship Day events on
June 30

Most accommodation is clustered along Sabang Beach. If surfing is your main goal, a beachfront surf camp or guesthouse (about
per night) is convenient, while a mid-range resort further back from the beach (about

) is a good choice if you want air conditioning and a pool. Inside Dicasalarin Cove there is one resort that feels like it has the whole cove to itself; it is pricier and set apart from town, making it suitable for travelers who want a quiet retreat.

The food here centers on seafood. Staples include kinilaw (fresh fish cured in vinegar and ginger), ginataan (dishes simmered in coconut milk), and charcoal-grilled fish, while suman (sticky rice cakes wrapped in banana leaf), coconut sweets, and dried fish sold at the market make good souvenirs. Sabang Beach has several smoothie and pasta cafes for surfers, where about
per meal is enough.

Among the long-established spots, Bay's Inn, in the middle of Sabang Beach, is a lodge with its own beachfront restaurant that's popular with surfers, while the four-star Costa Pacifica, with a pool and restaurant, gives its guests a discount on the Dicasalarin entrance fee. During the Suman Festival in
February
, streets and homes are decorated with finger-shaped suman hung up on display, and many kinds of suman are sold along the roadside.
There are a few ATMs in Baler town, but they can run out of cash during holidays. It's safer to withdraw plenty of cash before leaving Manila.
You can negotiate a surf lesson directly on the beach, but beginners tend to improve faster by taking 2–3 consecutive sessions with the same instructor.
Bring a rash guard and reef shoes. They protect you from the strong sun and reduce chafing from the board.
Mobile data works well in town and at Sabang Beach, but the signal is weak around Dicasalarin and the waterfall. Get your driver's contact number in advance.
By afternoon, the cliffs cast their shadow over Dicasalarin Cove's beach. Photos come out brightest in the late morning to around midday.
The waterfall trek crosses the river several times, so trekking shoes or aqua shoes that can get wet are better than sandals.
Return buses are busiest on Sunday afternoons. A good tip is to buy your return ticket as soon as you arrive.
Tourists entering Baler pay an environmental tourism fee (SEDF) of

per person (free for children 7 and under, 20% off for seniors and persons with disabilities). The same ticket gets you into the Museo de Baler and Doña Aurora's birth house, so keep it with you for your whole stay. Fees may change, so check the latest notices.
The National Museum of the Philippines Baler branch is free and opens at
. It makes a good stop after a morning surf session or a good addition to a rainy-day plan.
A guide is mandatory at Ditumabo Falls and the fee is charged per group, so teaming up with others at your lodging or on the beach lowers the cost per person.
Because the beach faces the open Pacific directly, rip currents (fast currents pulling swimmers out to sea) can form easily. Avoid swimming when a red flag is flying or when the waves are big.
During surf lessons, stay within the area your instructor assigns and avoid the experienced surfers' zone near the river mouth point.
During the rainy season and typhoon season, landslides can occur on the Baler–Bongabon mountain road, sometimes closing it to traffic.
The waterfall's flow can rise sharply after rain. If the sky upstream turns dark, leave the area immediately.
UV exposure is very strong at midday. Bring reef-safe sunscreen, a hat, and plenty of water.
Don't leave litter on the beach, and don't take shells or coral away with you.
During Super Typhoon Uwan in
November 2025

, part of Baler's seawall collapsed and waves cut the Baler–Casiguran road on the Dipaculao side. After a typhoon passes, check first with your lodging or the announcements of the Aurora Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (PDRRMO) whether the northern coast, including Dinadiawan, and the mountain roads are open.
